title: JPMorgan Doubles SpaceX Target to $500 as Shares Jump 8% on AI Compute Forecast

tickers.name: Space Exploration Technologies Corp. Class A Common Stock
Alphabet Inc. Class A Common Stock

summary:
JPMorgan more than doubled its price target on SpaceX to $500 from $240 and kept an Overweight rating, leading a wave of Wall Street upgrades as the shares rose 8% in premarket trading after third quarter results. The bank more than doubled its 2027 and 2028 financial estimates, forecasting $254 billion in 2027 revenue and 10 GW of computing capacity by the end of that year to support roughly $400 billion in ARR, while noting strategic merit in a potential merger with Tesla. Morgan Stanley set a $300 target with an Overweight rating, while Wells Fargo raised its target to $274 from $214, Citi to $240 from $200, UBS to $230 from $210, and Mizuho to $205 from $200.

The analyst revisions follow Elon Musk's post on X that "$1T in SpaceX revenue in 2028 is no longer impossible" and his earnings call projection that the company will add 10 GW of AI compute in 2027 to reach roughly 13 GW. SpaceX reported 1.7 GW of nameplate capacity at the end of September and guided to 2.5 GW to 3 GW by year end, with Musk planning to split compute roughly evenly between internal products and outside rental customers such as Google and Anthropic. Google's cloud agreement allows termination on 90 days' notice after Dec. 31.

Beneath SpaceX's headline $4.4 billion third quarter net profit, core operations generated about $2.8 billion in operating income after a $1.2 billion stock compensation charge tied to the Cursor acquisition, while interest income, other income and a tax benefit added roughly $1.6 billion. Cursor contributed $608 million in revenue between Aug. 14 and Sept. 30 inside the Super Intelligence division, which grew 830% from a year earlier to $7.56 billion and surpassed Starlink's $5.25 billion connectivity business. Cash and cash equivalents ended the quarter at $51.29 billion against consensus estimates of $91.2 billion, alongside $38.56 billion in marketable securities.

selectedTweets.text:
SpaceX is targeting another 10 GW of compute in 2027, reaching roughly 13 GW by year-end. Working backward from that target makes for an interesting thought experiment across deployment pace, chips, power, land and revenue. Commissioning the associated infrastructure and sustaining the economics would still require a substantial execution effort.

>Q4 broadly reconciles. SpaceX reported 1.7 GW at September-end and guides to 2.5–3 GW by year-end. That implies adding 0.8–1.3 GW in Q4, versus 0.3 GW in Q3. At the stated ~200k GB300s/month and ~2 kW per GPU at the server level, additions would be ~0.4 GW/month: 1.7 + 1.2 = 2.9 GW. Delivering that would put quarterly additions around or above the ~1 GW peers have disclosed, subject to comparable power definitions (1.2 GW AMZN 4Q25, MSFT 1GW in 2 recent Qs)

>Another 10 GW in 2027 implies averaging 2.5 GW a quarter. That’s over 8× Q3 and 1.9–3.1× the implied Q4 additions, sustained for a full year. For scale, it’s roughly one-fifth of SemiAnalysis’s already aggressive ~50 GW forecast for 2027 additions, assuming comparable scope and units. That forecast already anticipates substantial SpaceX expansion.

>An all-Rubin build would imply ~3m GPUs, or ~250k/month. GIGABYTE lists a representative NVL72 rack at 240 kW: 240 ÷ 72 = ~3.33 kW per GPU at the rack. Then 10m kW ÷ 3.33 = ~3m GPUs. That monthly requirement is only 25% above the stated ~200k Q4 cadence. Higher power per rack helps explain how GW additions could grow much faster than chip deliveries. Allocation, hardware mix and commissioning timing would still need to line up.

>Treating the target as 10 GW of IT load, a 1.25 PUE implies 12.5 GW of facility load. Add a 20% generation reserve and it becomes ~15 GW of installed generation. Those are illustrative assumptions. Warehouse conversions and behind-the-meter gas offer a route around grid queues, while in-house blade and vane casting could help turbine supply. Gas connections, air permits, cooling, electrical equipment and crews would still need to arrive on the same schedule. This might bridge to his 10GW IT target vs 20GW of power & cooling.

>At Colossus 1’s mapped density, 10 GW would occupy ~2,800 acres, equivalent to roughly 30 Colossus 1s. That uses Epoch’s ~340 MW IT on ~96 acres and excludes off-site generation. Distributed across several locations, the acreage seems more manageable than getting enough sites ready for 2027. Southaven’s existing Clean Air Act litigation illustrates one potential source of delay.

>The revenue sensitivity is enormous. Musk described a roughly 50-50 split between internal compute and rental. At 13 GW, fully renting the external half at $25bn/GW/year would imply ~$163bn of exit annualized rental revenue; at $50bn/GW, ~$325bn. Those illustrative pricing inputs use the upper ends of different Nebius deal cohorts. For context, Q3 SI Solutions & Infrastructure revenue ex-Cursor annualizes to ~$25.6bn, or ~$16.5bn/GW across an estimated average fleet of 1.55 GW. That includes other SI revenue and internal-use capacity in the denominator, so it cannot be read as a rental yield. SpaceX has demonstrated speed and has substantial liquidity. Contract duration still matters for funding: Google’s agreement permits termination on 90 days’ notice after December 31. 

By the way all of the build also comes alongside Starship and satellite expansion and a potential Tesla merger. Q4 delivery would establish a much stronger starting pace. The next useful detail would be a monthly/quarterly schedule connecting GPU allocations with commissioned sites, usable power and funding.
selectedTweets.quotedTweetText:
Another +10 GW of compute for SpaceX/xAI in 2027 is physically and technically possible in definition. Delivering it on that timeline, alongside everything else Musk is taking on, seems ambitious to say the least.  

They reported 1.7 GW of nameplate compute at September-end, up from 1.4 GW in June. Adding 10 GW next year means averaging 2.5 GW per quarter, over 8x last quarter’s additions. That’s more than 3x their expected ~3 GW year-end fleet added in one year.  

Using the high-end SemiAnalysis’s ~50 GW global forecast for 2027 additions as a rough benchmark, one player would account for ~20% of the buildout. The power definitions need to match (e.g., unclear if Elon is using IT or facility load; if IT add another 20% GW for the cooling/electrical/overhead which amplifies the problem), but that’s a huge share of an already exceptionally bullish industry forecast. 

If 10 GW means IT load, an illustrative ~3 kW per GPU, including allocated system overhead, implies ~3.3 million GPUs (which begs of the Q of can you get that many chips). At an assumed $30–50 billion per IT GW, it would also mean $300–500 billion of investment (which begs the Q of can you finance them in this environment).

They’ve demonstrated exceptional construction speed. Industrial conversions and behind-the-meter generation give them a credible way around long grid timelines. There may be much more equipment secured and construction underway than is publicly visible. 

But turbines still leave gas delivery, land, permits, transformers, cooling, construction crews and commissioning. Buying acreage in Texas, Mississippi and Tennessee seems achievable. Getting enough sites approved, equipped and operating on that schedule is much harder. They’re competing with hyperscalers and other AI developers for the same constrained chips, equipment and skilled labor. 

The political environment is getting harder too. Power bills, water, noise and emissions are feeding bipartisan opposition, moratoriums and litigation. SpaceX’s existing Southaven power project is already defending an environmental lawsuit. 

Financing also faces greater scrutiny. CoreWeave’s 2031 bond yield touched almost 16% last week as investors reassessed its debt risk. For projects requiring this much capital upfront, delays extend the gap between spending and revenue.  All of that while bringing more manufacturing in-house and scaling Starship. A Tesla merger, if it happens, would add another major undertaking.

I’ve learned to avoid calling Elon’s targets impossible. I’m still skeptical of this deadline without seeing how much of the next 10 GW already has sites, permits, equipment allocations and funded construction behind it.  Late here, eager to dig further into the project pipeline tomorrow.
